questions.q: In the naive failure matrix, why is "queue down" worse than "database down", although both answered 500?
questions.explain: A failure after a side effect is the dangerous kind: the answer says "nothing happened" when something did. The customer's natural retry turns it into a duplicate.
options: Queues are more important than databases
The order had already been saved, so the customer was told it failed although it exists, and pressing "Pay" again creates a second order
A queue outage lasts longer than a database outage
The 500 from the queue leaked a stack trace

questions.q: Before adding timeouts, retries or breakers, what does the lesson ask you to decide for each dependency?
questions.explain: Those three answers decide the mechanism: fail fast for critical dependencies, a fallback for optional ones, retries only for safe operations. They are business decisions, so they come first.
options: Which cloud region it runs in
Whether it is needed for a correct answer, what users can still get when it is down, and whether calling it twice is safe
How many retries it can survive
Which programming language it is written in

questions.q: A timeout wrapper uses only Promise.race with a timer and never aborts anything. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Promises cannot be cancelled from outside. Giving up waiting is not stopping the work; only a signal the work listens to (or a driver's cancel call) stops it.
options: The caller waits forever
The caller is answered on time, but the work keeps running: it still holds connections and may still write data
The work is cancelled twice
Nothing: Promise.race cancels the losing promise

questions.q: Checkout calls four services in a row, each with a 2-second timeout, and the checkout page promises an answer within 2 seconds. What is the fix?
questions.explain: Separate timeouts add up. A deadline is shared by the whole request, so the total wait is bounded no matter how many calls it makes.
options: Lower every timeout to 500 ms
Raise the checkout budget to 8 seconds
Give the request a deadline and give each call min(its own limit, time left), cancelling everything when the deadline passes
Call the four services with retries

questions.q: How should you choose a dependency's timeout?
questions.explain: Below normal latency, the timeout fails healthy calls; far above it, it protects nothing. The slow tail, not the average, is what normal traffic actually needs.
options: Always 30 seconds, the common default
As short as possible, such as 1 ms
A little above the slow tail of normal latency (for example the 99th percentile), measured, and reviewed when latency changes
Twice the average latency

questions.q: Which failure is worth retrying?
questions.explain: Only transient failures can succeed on a later attempt. Invalid input, missing records and declined cards will fail the same way every time.
options: 400 Bad Request: the body is missing a field
404 Not Found: the order id does not exist
402: the card was declined
503 Service Unavailable from an instance that is restarting

questions.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
questions.explain: Without randomness, every client computes the same waits. Jitter spreads the retries over time, turning spikes into a trickle.
options: It makes each retry faster
Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together, hitting the recovering service in synchronized waves
It reduces the number of attempts
It is required for idempotency

questions.q: The browser, the gateway and the orders service each retry up to 3 attempts. The database is down. How many database calls can one click cause, and what is the usual fix?
questions.explain: Retries multiply across layers: 3 × 3 × 3. Retrying at the layer closest to the dependency, with a retry budget, keeps an outage from tripling its own load.
options: 3; nothing needs fixing
9; add jitter
27; retry at one layer only and let the others fail fast
27; add a fourth layer of retries

questions.q: A POST /orders call times out. Why must the client not simply retry it?
questions.explain: After a timeout the client cannot know whether the work happened. Retrying a non-idempotent write is only safe when the server can recognise the repeat.
options: POST requests cannot be sent twice
The server may have created the order before the answer was lost, so a retry can create a second one, unless the request carries an idempotency key
The server will reject the second request automatically
Timeouts only happen for GET requests

questions.q: What does a circuit breaker add that a timeout does not?
questions.explain: A timeout still makes every call wait for the limit. An open breaker skips the call entirely, which protects both sides.
options: It makes each call faster when the dependency is healthy
During an outage it fails calls immediately without touching the dependency, so callers do not wait and the dependency gets room to recover
It retries failed calls automatically
It caches the last successful answer

questions.q: Why does the lesson's breaker use a rolling window of recent results instead of "open after 3 failures in a row"?
questions.explain: A failure rate over recent calls describes health much better than a streak. minimumCalls stops it from judging on too few results.
options: Rolling windows use less memory
A single success between failures resets a consecutive counter, so a dependency failing 90% of calls might never trip it
Consecutive counters cannot be tested
The window makes the breaker open sooner in every case

questions.q: Why does the half-open breaker let exactly one probe through?
questions.explain: The probe asks "are you back?" gently. Only when it succeeds does full traffic return.
options: To save memory
If every waiting call went through at once, a service that has just recovered would be hit by a flood and could fail again
Because JavaScript cannot run two calls at once
To make the breaker close faster

questions.q: A breaker around the payments API opens whenever a card is declined (402). What is wrong?
questions.explain: Only errors that indicate an unhealthy dependency (5xx, timeouts, refused connections, and 429) should count. Business outcomes are successes from the breaker's point of view.
options: Nothing: any error is a failure
A decline means the API is working correctly; counting it lets a few customers with expired cards cut payments off for everyone
402 should retry, not open the breaker
The window is too large

questions.q: The rates API hangs and ShopFlow's single pool of outgoing calls is full of rate requests. Checkout, which needs only the healthy database, is refused. What prevents this?
questions.explain: Bulkheads isolate capacity, like watertight compartments in a ship. One slow dependency floods its compartment, not the whole service.
options: A longer timeout for the rates API
More retries for checkout
A bulkhead: a separate limited pool per dependency, so the rates API can only fill its own
A cache in front of the database

questions.q: With a full bulkhead, extra rate requests were "rejected at once" instead of waiting. Why is that good?
questions.explain: Waiting in line for a dependency that is not answering only spreads the outage. A quick "no" plus a fallback keeps the rest of the page fast.
options: Rejected requests are retried automatically
A fast rejection frees the server for work it can do, and the page can fall back (for example to naira only) immediately
It makes the rates API recover sooner
Browsers prefer errors to slow answers

questions.q: The permissions service is down. What is the right fallback for "can this user refund an order?"
questions.explain: Degrade features, never security. A fallback that grants access during an outage is an attacker's favourite outage.
options: Allow it, so customers are not blocked
Allow it for users who were allowed yesterday
Deny (or hold for later), and tell the user the action is temporarily unavailable
Retry until the permissions service answers

questions.q: Why must a liveness probe not check the database?
questions.explain: Liveness answers "is this process stuck?", and a restart is its remedy. Readiness answers "should I get traffic?", which is where dependency checks belong.
options: Database checks are too slow
When the database fails, every instance fails liveness and the platform restarts them all in a loop, which cannot fix the database and adds a restart storm
Liveness probes cannot open network connections
The database has its own liveness probe

questions.q: An instance receives SIGTERM during a deploy. What should it do first?
questions.explain: New traffic must stop arriving before the instance stops accepting it. Then it finishes in-flight work, drains workers, and closes dependencies last.
options: Close the database connection
Exit immediately with code 0
Stop reporting ready, and keep serving briefly while the load balancer notices
Reject all in-flight requests

questions.q: In the published @zudojs/runtime, why did the lesson's /ready probe check runtime.state === "running" as well as runtime.ready?
questions.explain: Readiness means "my dependencies are fine and I intend to serve". The lifecycle state carries the second half, so the probe must include it.
options: Because runtime.ready is always false
Running the readiness checks during shutdown recomputes ready from the checks alone, so a stopping instance with a healthy database would report ready
Because runtime.state is faster to read
It is only a style preference

questions.q: A worker claims a job and its process is killed. stalledAfter returns the job to the queue and another worker runs it. What must the job handler therefore be?
questions.explain: Crash recovery means running the job again. Store what you did (a booking reference, a payment id) and check it first, so a second run does not repeat the side effect.
options: Fast
Idempotent, because the dead worker may have done part or all of the work before it died
Written in TypeScript
Registered twice

questions.q: What does registering the loyalty plugin's component with critical: false change?
questions.explain: Optional means the application is useful without it. The component:failed event is where the alert goes, and every caller must check whether the plugin is running.
options: The plugin starts faster
If it fails to start, the application still starts without it; you must alert on the failure and make the code that uses it cope with its absence
The plugin is retried forever
The plugin runs in a separate process

questions.q: Why validate configuration at startup, before the instance reports ready?
questions.explain: Failing fast is most useful when the platform can see it. Readiness is the signal the deploy system uses to continue or stop the rollout.
options: Validation is faster at startup
A new instance that never becomes ready stops a rolling deploy while old instances keep serving, turning a bad setting into a failed deploy instead of an outage
Configuration cannot be read later
So the error message includes a stack trace

questions.q: A customer closes the tab while a sales report is being built. With @zudojs/http, how does the server stop the work?
questions.explain: Cancellation only works if the signal is passed all the way down. Each call that accepts it stops when the customer leaves.
options: It cannot; the report always finishes
The request's signal aborts when the client disconnects; passing it to every call (timers, fetch, queries) stops the remaining work
The server sends a 499 status
The report is cached for later

questions.q: Why does the chaos test use a seeded random generator instead of Math.random?
questions.explain: Randomness finds unexpected combinations; the seed makes them repeatable. Print the seed of every random run so you can replay it.
options: Seeded generators are more random
Math.random is not available in Node.js
The same seed produces the same faults every run, so a failure found once can be reproduced and kept as a regression test
It makes the test run faster

questions.q: Which of these is an invariant for the checkout chaos test?
questions.explain: An invariant must hold whatever breaks. Outcomes such as 201 vary with the faults; what must never vary is the relationship between the answer and the saved state.
options: The database is always up
Checkout returns 201 in every run
Every 503 answer saved no order, so a customer's retry cannot create a duplicate
Each run takes less than 10 ms

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The delay doubles from attempt to attempt, starting at the base (attempt 1 uses 2⁰), and maxDelay caps it at 1,000. Without jitter, this is deterministic.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A fixed backoff waits the same time before every retry. It is simple, but many clients failing together keep retrying together.
questions.code:
import { calculateRetryDelay } from "@zudojs/queue";

console.log([1, 2, 3].map((attempt) => calculateRetryDelay(attempt, { type: "fixed", delay: 250 })).join(" "));

questions.q: Full jitter with a fake random generator. What does this print?
questions.explain: Full jitter picks a wait between 0 and the backoff ceiling. With a controlled generator the result is predictable, which is exactly why the lesson passes the generator in.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The gateway tries the service twice, and each service attempt tries the database 4 times: 2 × 4 = 8 calls for one request.

questions.q: A breaker that opens after 2 consecutive failures, on a fake clock. What does this print?
questions.explain: Two failures open it; the third call fails fast. At 1500 the probe fails, so it reopens at 1500 and the next call fails fast. At 3000 the pause is over again, the probe succeeds and it closes.
options: error error fast-fail error fast-fail ok closed
error error ok error ok ok closed
error error fast-fail ok ok ok closed
error error fast-fail error fast-fail ok open

questions.explain: The race rejected after 20 ms, but nothing stopped the slow work, which finished at 60 ms anyway. That is zombie work: the caller gave up, the work did not.
options:
timed out false
finished later: true

timed out false
finished later: false

finished later: true

timed out true
finished later: true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The work checks the signal before each step. After step 2 the signal is aborted with a custom reason, so step 3 never runs and the reason is thrown.
options: client disconnected 1,2
done 1,2,3
client disconnected 1,2,3
AbortError 1,2

questions.explain: Two calls fill the bulkhead; the next two are rejected at once. When the first two finish, capacity is free again.
options: ok ok rejected rejected | later: ok
ok ok ok ok | later: ok
ok rejected rejected rejected | later: ok
ok ok rejected rejected | later: rejected

questions.explain: The same seed always gives the same sequence; a different seed gives a different one. That is what makes a chaos run reproducible.
options: true false
false false
true true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Classifying by error class keeps retry and breaker decisions out of message text. A plain Error is most likely a bug in your own code: retrying it only repeats the bug.
options: ServiceUnavailableError:true ValidationError:false TimeoutError:true Error:false
ServiceUnavailableError:true ValidationError:true TimeoutError:true Error:true
ServiceUnavailableError:true ValidationError:false TimeoutError:false Error:false
ServiceUnavailableError:false ValidationError:false TimeoutError:true Error:false

questions.q: Write retry(work, attempts, isRetryable). It calls work(attempt) until it succeeds, the error is not retryable, or attempts is used up, and logs attempt N failed: MESSAGE for each failure that will be retried. (No waiting is needed here.)
questions.explain: The permanent error is thrown on its first occurrence. Checking "retryable" before "attempts left" or after makes no difference to the result, but logging only retried failures keeps the log honest.
questions.expected:
attempt 1 failed: 503 rates unavailable
attempt 2 failed: 503 rates unavailable
rate 105
gave up: 400 currency XYZ unknown

questions.q: Write withTimeout(ms, work): it creates an AbortController, aborts it after ms with new Error("timed out"), passes the signal to work, and rejects as soon as the signal aborts even if the work ignores it. Clear the timer when done.
questions.explain: The caller gets "timed out" in both slow cases, on time. The third work function would have seen the abort, but its answer arrives after the race has already rejected: work that checks the signal should stop, not return.

questions.q: Complete createBreaker(maxFailures, openMs, now). It returns call(work) and state(). After maxFailures consecutive failures it opens: calls throw new Error("open") without running work until openMs have passed; then one call is tried (half-open), which closes it on success or reopens it on failure.
questions.explain: The third call failed fast although the dependency had recovered: that is the cost of the pause. After 100 ms of fake time the probe succeeded and normal traffic resumed. A fake clock makes the whole scenario instant and repeatable.

questions.q: Write createBulkhead(max) returning run(work): at most max works run at once; any extra call rejects immediately with new Error("full"). Capacity must be released even when the work fails.
questions.explain: The finally is what releases the slot after the failure; without it, one failed call would leave the bulkhead full forever and "c" would be rejected.

questions.q: Use calculateRetryDelay from @zudojs/queue (exponential, base 100, max 800) and the given fake random values to print the full-jitter wait for attempts 1 to 5, each rounded, joined by spaces.
questions.explain: The ceilings are 100, 200, 400, 800 and 800 (capped). Full jitter multiplies each by a random number between 0 and 1. Passing the random values in makes the schedule testable.

questions.q: Write readyStatus(checks, lifecycle). checks maps names to booleans; lifecycle is a state such as "running" or "stopping". Return "200" when every check passes and the state is "running"; otherwise "503 " followed by the reasons joined with ", " (failed checks by name, then state=STATE if not running).
questions.explain: Readiness has two halves: dependencies are fine, and the instance intends to serve. A stopping instance with a healthy database must still answer 503, or the load balancer keeps sending it customers.

questions.q: Each chaos run produced { run, status, orders, receipts }. Print every violation of these invariants: a 201 must have exactly 1 order and 1 receipt; a 503 must have 0 orders. Print run N: PROBLEM lines, then violations: COUNT.
questions.explain: Run 3 is the double-order bug; run 4 is a lost receipt. Invariants check relationships between the answer and the saved state, which is why they catch bugs that "did it return 201?" never would.
questions.expected:
run 3: 503 but an order was saved
run 4: 201 with 1 orders and 0 receipts
violations: 2

questions.q: Write priceLabel(kobo, rate, now) where rate is { ngnPerGhs, at } or undefined. Show ₦X.XX, and add (about GH₵Y.YY) only when a rate exists and is at most one hour (3,600,000 ms) old.
questions.explain: A stale fallback needs a limit. An hour-old exchange rate is a fair courtesy price; a week-old one is wrong. Beyond the limit, degrade further: show naira only.
